name: Example: Computing Mass or Charge Using Polar Coordinates
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/f0db928874dba8d872cde46d1467686010f3484765b2d7e39807b5a32a131b09.png)

Find the total charge $Q$ of a copper plate that occupies the region $D$ shown above, and has charge density 

$$
\rho (x,y) = \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}  .
$$
worked_solution:
First, notice that the region $D$ represents one-quarter of the disk of radius $3$ centered at 
$\left(0,0\right).$

The total charge $Q$ of an object occupying the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y) =  \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$ is given by

$$
Q = \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}  \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \rho(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ \rho(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

The following equations connect Cartesian and polar coordinates:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the curve $x^2+y^2=9$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =9 \\ {r}^{2} & =9 \\ r & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \pi \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r]\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\frac{9}{2}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =18[-1-0] \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the quarter-disk is $Q = - 18.$
